channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: Americans sure are normal enough to live in Adelaide
item.description: Returning from California, Keith Dunstan argues the United States is one of the most normal places on earth, and that Australian country motel breakfasts — three-ply toast, instant coffee — make a sorry contrast to American roadside hotcakes.

item.title: The Punks at the Automatic Teller
item.description: A visit to Melbourne's punk hairdressers reveals the engineering behind the Apache-strip, the bobtail, and the scrunch, all of it driven not by political protest but by the desire to look like Boy George.

item.title: I've really had an earful...
item.description: A comic survey of the earring boom, from Elton John's diamond studs and Queen Elizabeth II's pearls to the domestic hazards of pierced ears in a household of daughters.

item.title: Know him? We've just kissed.
item.description: A 1984 photograph of Prince Charles kissing Prince Edward on the cheek prompts a survey of the social kissing boom, from Brezhnev lifting Kissinger bodily off the ground to the art of the cocktail party fake-kiss.

item.title: Stand by as the get-away becomes a give-away
item.description: A tour through airline brochures reveals the extraordinary lengths carriers are going to in 1984 to win custom, from Dom Perignon in Waterford Crystal to Delft liqueur houses and Sony Walkman headsets.

item.title: Norm and I Adore Satire and Yoga
item.description: Barry Humphries returns to Melbourne from London, more polished and confident, with a new show at the Comedy Theatre, an updated Mrs Norm Everage who now does yoga and hangs her own pasta on the clothesline, and stories of waiting outside the Savoy in drag to ambush the Prime Minister.

item.title: You Can't Get Much Lusher
item.description: The Fabulous Lido, a lavish theatre-restaurant in Melbourne's old Savoy building, is about to open, with millionaire ex-dancer David Hamilton McIlwraith pouring half a million pounds into gold mosaic tiles, chandeliers imported from Egypt and long-legged hand-picked showgirls.

item.title: Keeping up with Carnaby Street
item.description: British fashion designers Roger Nelson and Jean Muir arrive in Melbourne to present the mod Regency look for men, double-breasted with six buttons and floral shirts, and confirm that Melbourne's Lord Henry's Gear store in Russell Street is right up with the latest in Carnaby Street.

item.title: Return of Norm and Edna Everage
item.description: Welcomes Barry Humphries home from London for a nine-night Assembly Hall season, recounting his elaborate public pranks, including the "Ashburton Line" breakfast-in-a-carriage stunt and slices of ham hidden in a David Jones bargain sale.

item.title: To the Spencer Street Station
item.description: Compares the muted arrival of the new Southern Aurora express at Spencer Street with the wild 1883 celebrations when Melbourne and Sydney's rail lines first met at Albury, then covers Victoria's new ban on tattooing minors.

item.title: Wild Life in Suburbia
item.description: A Brotherhood of St Laurence survey of a Melbourne housing estate puts hard numbers on Barry Humphries' Mrs Everage caricature, finding suburban Melburnians were overwhelmingly stay-at-home, TV-watching and incurious.

item.title: The Oyohus of the Pram Belt
item.description: A tour of the outer-suburban display-home craze gripping Melbourne in 1964, from the traffic-snarled exposition villages of East Doncaster to the Brotherhood of St Laurence's grim report on 55,000 families unable to afford decent housing.

item.title: O, the Opulence of O!
item.description: A behind-the-scenes tour of Reg Ansett's Austarama TV studio at Nunawading, showcasing the opulent new Channel O before its August 1964 launch, with a pointed reminder of Ansett's 1963 promise to show Australians what Australia has to offer.

item.title: The Monash Story: Keeping Them Down on the Farm
item.description: A portrait of Monash University three years after its unexpectedly early opening, examining its car-dependent Clayton campus, its race to become the world's fastest-growing university, its chronic underfunding, and the outsized personalities shaping its character.

item.title: Loyalty that opens cheque books and office doors
item.description: A review of John McLaren's book 'Our Troubled Schools' examines Melbourne's public-school pecking order, from Geelong Grammar at the top for the landed aristocracy through to junior technical school students at the bottom, and the intolerable dilemma facing parents over where to educate their children.

item.title: One more week
item.description: A Melbourne arts round-up taking in the National Gallery of Victoria's new building and its first temporary exhibition, a Jawaharlal Nehru memorial at Sydney's Australia Square, Brisbane's new Sunday entertainment laws, and filmmaker John Heyer's latest attempt to raise money for an Australian feature film.

item.title: Dawn of a New Golden Age
item.description: A behind-the-scenes account of the lavish promotional campaign Hoyts mounted for the Melbourne premiere of Goldfinger, from painted-gold television models and purloined Bond-girl display panels to kits containing white roses and toy revolvers.

item.title: Now Watch Out for Those Inside Stories!
item.description: Keith Dunstan enrols at the Australian Academy of Investigation, a Collins Street school for private detectives run by a former Melbourne CIB man, and is disillusioned to find the work is mostly insurance claims and divorce surveillance, not espionage.

item.title: Goodbye to the Glaci
item.description: Farewells Melbourne's Glaciarium after fire destroyed the pioneering ice rink, recalling its genteel opening in 1906, orchestras, speed skaters and eventual defeat by St Moritz and changing fashions.

item.title: All the Fun of the Ferry
item.description: A report on Melbourne's Moomba festival, tracing how it grew from the old Eight-hour Day trade union procession into a city-wide holiday spectacle, with Sydney's Manly ferry North Head the unexpected hit of the week on the Yarra.

item.title: Dogs Chasing Each Other's Tails
item.description: The 14th Australian Architectural Convention debates the chaotic state of Melbourne's planning, with Harry Seidler lamenting the two-to-one height formula and architects mourning the imminent demolition of Walter Burley Griffin's Capitol Theatre for a shopping arcade.

item.title: Just an Anonymous Airport
item.description: The Federal Government's failure to fund terminal buildings at Melbourne's new Tullamarine airport reignites the Melbourne-Sydney rivalry, with Melbourne's Tullamarine boosters warning the city risks disappearing from international air maps entirely.

item.title: Bolte Plays Ring-a-rosy
item.description: Melbourne's almost total absence of freeways, while Sydney and American cities forge ahead, traced to the Victorian Country Party's stranglehold on the Legislative Council and its repeated blocking of Henry Bolte's road-funding proposals.

item.title: Batman Crosses the Murray
item.description: A visit to Sydney forces a grudging admission that the city is gaining an edge on Melbourne, with superior old and new buildings, easier taxi access, cheaper public transport and a Sydney Opera House that, from a distance at least, looks glorious.

item.title: Among the Pasties
item.description: A tour of Sydney's King's Cross strip clubs, from the Pink Pussy Cat to the Crazy Horse, appraising the performers, the audiences and the bizarre economics of a world where a good stripper earns seventy pounds a week and can appear at three clubs a night.

item.title: Wanted, a Civic Symbol
item.description: The case for Melbourne's proposed Lower Yarra bridge as the city's long-missing civic symbol, with a detailed comparison of its planned dimensions against the Sydney Harbour Bridge and a sidelight on the Rebecca Riots as a precedent for toll-gate fury.

item.title: Which City is in Front...?
item.description: A survey of the Melbourne versus Sydney rivalry, examining competing newspaper claims about population growth, migration, new industries, building completions and personal income, prompted by the CIA-level precision with which LBJ's visit was split equally between the two cities.

item.title: A Viscount, a Viscount, a Viscount . . .
item.description: Profiles bandleader Tommy Davidson, Melbourne's leading writer of singing television commercials, from his award-winning Viscount cigarette jingle to a £5500 TV shoot with a 46-piece orchestra.

item.title: Rembrandt and Phar Lap
item.description: A reluctant Melburnian tourist takes a sightseeing coach tour of his own city, from Ned Kelly's gaol to the National Gallery, and finds Phar Lap draws more attention than the Rembrandt.

item.title: Now They Call Him "Satchmo" Bolte
item.description: Traces the Exhibition Building's rise from would-be demolition target to beloved 1963 Trade Fair venue via its riotous 1880s exhibition history, then catches Henry Bolte earning the nickname "Satchmo" over a misquoted Anthony Trollope line about Victorian boasting.
